title: Risk: is this approach effective, and why?
blurb: Judge whether risks are identified, assessed and responded to well in a scenario, and pick the reason that really explains the verdict.
question: Fernhollow Foods has a very low appetite for allergen risk. The project manager proposes to accept the threat of sesame cross-contamination because controls are costly. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?

teach.h: Three tests for any risk decision
teach.body: When a question asks whether risk is being managed well, test it three ways. Does it follow the technique: identify (as cause, event and effect), assess, plan, implement, with communication throughout? Does it respect who sets what: the business sets risk appetite, the board sets risk tolerance from it? Does it fit this project: proportionate, aware of decision bias and using data where it helps? A 'No' usually breaks one of these; a 'Yes' must be explained by the one the scenario is about.

teach.caption: The first four steps are sequential; communicate runs alongside them through existing reports (9.3.1).

teach.h: Responses and how to spot them
head: Threat / opportunity
Spot it in the scenario
rows: The situation is made certain: cause removed, or gain locked in
Definite action now changes probability or impact; some risk remains
A third party, such as an insurer, bears the financial impact
Pain and gain shared with a partner, often by contract
No action now; the risk is kept under watch
Actions planned now, used if the risk occurs
teach.caption: Response types, table 9.1. Raising the chance of a gain is enhance, not exploit, unless the gain becomes certain.

rows.label: What it is
values: Amount and type of risk accepted

teach.caption: 9.2.1. The risk budget funds risk responses; the change budget funds approved changes.
An illustration only: the project's own scales live in its risk management approach. Proximity and velocity also affect priority.

teach.h: Decision bias and the use of data
teach.body: Bias is natural but can harm risk decisions. Loss aversion values avoiding a loss over an equal gain. Optimism bias discounts bad news and assumes success. Groupthink puts harmony before dissent or the right decision. Proximity bias treats near-term risks as more important than later ones. Good practice recognizes these and uses data and analytics, such as past performance or call volumes, to identify and assess risks more objectively.

teach.h: Judging a risk entry or action

root.label: A proposed risk entry or action

teach.body: Fernhollow Foods has never handled sesame. Project manager Nadia Osei registers the threat that sesame residue may reach other lines, causing an allergen recall. Accepting it would clash with the board's very low appetite, so she recommends avoid: Megan Cho's chefs reformulate that recipe without sesame. Charlotte Vane insists all six recipes will be ready; Nadia uses consumer panel scores to counter the optimism, and agrees a contingent plan to launch four recipes, Harbridge's minimum, if two are not ready.

items: Decide the verdict from the scenario facts: is it uncertain, described well, within appetite, set by the right role?
Cross out the two options with the wrong verdict.
Of the two left, pick the reason that explains THIS situation, not just a true statement about risk.
Check the role: appetite from the business, tolerance from the board, procedure run by the PM.

teach.text: Traps: (1) enhance raises the chance of a gain, exploit makes it certain; reduce changes probability or impact, avoid removes the risk; (2) risk tolerance is set by the project board from the business's appetite, not by the PM; (3) the risk budget funds responses, the change budget funds changes; (4) a risk that has already happened is an issue.

items: Good risk practice follows identify, assess, plan, implement, with communication throughout.
Responses must fit the appetite: accepting a threat the business has a very low appetite for is poor practice.
Assess the combined risk profile against tolerance, not only single risks.
Name the bias: loss aversion, optimism, groupthink, proximity; counter it with data.
Right verdict AND the reason that explains the scenario.

summary: You can now judge risk identification, assessment and responses in a scenario against the technique, the appetite and tolerance rules and decision bias. You can also choose the reason that genuinely explains why an approach is or is not appropriate.

A.q: Carrowford City Council's half marathon project is in its build-up stage. A threat is that heavy rain on race weekend makes the riverside festival site unusable, losing stall income. The project manager buys event cancellation insurance that pays out the lost income if this happens. Which type of response is being used, and why?
options: Reduce, because it lowers the chance of rain
Accept, because the weather cannot be controlled
Transfer, because an insurer bears the cost impact
Share, because the insurer gains if no claim is made
A.why: A transfer response passes all or part of the financial impact of a threat to a third party, such as an insurer (9.2.3.1, table 9.1).

whyNot.0: Insurance does not change the probability of rain; it moves the financial impact.
whyNot.1: Accepting means taking no action now, but here definite action (insurance) has been taken.
whyNot.3: Sharing is a pain and gain arrangement with a partner; an insurance premium is a transfer of financial impact.

A.q: Tarnside College's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design stage. A third offshore wind operator may pledge apprentice places if it is impressed by the centre. Project manager Leah Whitfield arranges site visits and design briefings for the operator to raise the chance of a pledge. Which response is this, and why?
options: Enhance, because it raises the chance of the gain
Exploit, because it makes the extra pledge certain
Share, because the operator also gains from the centre
Accept, because the operator decides in the end
A.why: Enhance takes definite action now to increase the probability or impact of an opportunity; the pledge is still uncertain (9.2.3.1, table 9.1).

whyNot.1: Exploit would make the gain certain; the operator may still decide not to pledge.
whyNot.2: Sharing is a pain and gain arrangement agreed with a partner, which is not described here.
whyNot.3: Accepting means taking no action now, but Leah is taking definite action to improve the odds.

A.q: At a Fernhollow Kitchen board meeting, two board members privately doubt that six recipes will be ready for launch. They say nothing, because the rest of the board is enthusiastic and they do not want to spoil the mood. Which decision bias is most evident, and why?
options: Loss aversion, because the listing fee would be lost
Proximity bias, because the launch week is near
Optimism bias, because the chefs underestimated work
Groupthink, because harmony is put before dissent
A.why: Groupthink is valuing group cohesion over dissent or the right decision; the members suppress their doubts to keep harmony (9.2.4).

whyNot.0: The fee is at stake, but nothing suggests members are weighing a loss more heavily than a gain.
whyNot.1: Proximity bias treats near-term risks as more important; the issue here is silence to keep harmony.
whyNot.2: The scenario does not say the chefs underestimated; it describes members suppressing doubts.

B.q: Brennan Mutual's Project Skyline is in initiation. The board wants money set aside to rent temporary rack space in Leeds, to be used if wave 3 slips past the lease end date. Where should this money come from?
options: The change budget, held by the change authority
The risk budget, to fund this contingent plan
Stage cost tolerance for the wave migration stage
Project cost tolerance held by the business layer
B.why: The risk budget is money set aside to fund specific responses to threats and opportunities, such as contingent plans (ch 9).

whyNot.0: The change budget funds approved changes to the baseline, not responses to risks.
whyNot.2: Tolerance is a permissible deviation before escalation, not money to fund a planned response.
whyNot.3: Project tolerance sets limits for escalation to the business layer; it is not a fund for responses.

B.q: Wenmoor Community Health's project is near the end of its design and pilot preparation stage. Project manager Ellie Chandran has assessed each risk on its own. She now totals the likely effect of all open threats on the pilot start date and compares it with the stage time tolerance. Which step of the risk technique is she carrying out?
options: Identify: context and objectives
Plan: evaluating the responses
Implement: reviewing the responses
Assess: the combined risk profile
B.why: Assessing includes understanding the combined risk profile: the aggregate exposure compared with tolerances and appetite (9.3.1).

whyNot.0: Defining context and objectives happens at the start of identification, before risks are assessed.
whyNot.1: Planning identifies and evaluates responses; Ellie is measuring overall exposure, not choosing responses.
whyNot.2: Implementing involves carrying out responses and checking they work, not totalling exposure.

B.q: Calderbrook's Permits Online project is in discovery and alpha. Project manager Hannah Okoro uses the contact centre's call records to estimate how likely it is that residents over 75 will not use the online service. Which part of the risk practice guidance is she applying, and why?
options: Use of data, because evidence informs the assessment
Risk planning, because it sets the risk appetite
Proximity, because older residents are an early risk
Risk control, because it chooses the risk response
B.why: The guidance encourages data and analytics to identify and assess risks; the call records give evidence for the probability estimate (9.3.2.6).

whyNot.1: Risk appetite is set by the business, and the scenario is about estimating probability, not appetite.
whyNot.2: Proximity is about when a risk may occur; Hannah is estimating likelihood from data.
whyNot.3: Hannah is assessing the risk; no response has yet been chosen.

C.q: Fernhollow Foods' board has a very low appetite for food safety and allergen risk. One recipe uses sesame, which has never been handled on site. Project manager Nadia Osei proposes to accept the threat of cross-contamination and keep it under review, because extra cleaning controls are costly and the probability is low. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
options: Yes, because accept suits risks with a low probability
Yes, because the risk owner may choose the response
No, because it does not fit the very low appetite
No, because accepted risks move to the issue register
C.why: Responses must reflect the business's risk appetite, applied by the board through tolerance; accepting a food safety threat clashes with a very low appetite for that kind of risk (9.2.1, 9.2.3).

whyNot.0: Accept can suit low-probability threats, but that does not outweigh a very low appetite for allergen risk.
whyNot.1: The risk owner manages the response, but it must still fit the appetite and tolerance set above them.
whyNot.3: Accepted risks stay in the risk register and are monitored; they do not become issues.

C.q: Brennan Mutual's Project Skyline is about to enter its wave migration stage. Because the board meets monthly, project manager Mairi Campbell sets the risk tolerance for the stage herself, based on the aggregated exposure shown in the risk register. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
options: Yes, because combined exposure should drive tolerance
Yes, because the PM manages the stage day to day
No, because the business layer sets every tolerance
No, because the board sets it from the appetite
C.why: Risk tolerance is set by the project board based on the business's overall risk appetite, not by the project manager or from current exposure (9.2.1).

whyNot.0: Combined exposure is compared with tolerance; it is not the basis for setting it.
whyNot.1: The PM manages day to day within tolerances that the board sets.
whyNot.2: The business layer sets project tolerances and appetite; the board sets stage tolerances.

C.q: Carrowford City Council has a corporate risk management policy with standard scales, categories and reporting rules. During initiation of the half marathon project, project manager Kezia Oduya builds the project's risk management approach on these council standards rather than inventing new ones. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because it removes the need for a risk register
Yes, because business policy should shape the approach
No, because each project should set out its own risk scales
No, because the board must approve new scales in DP
C.why: Identifying risks starts by understanding the context: the business's policies, standards and procedures shape the project's risk management approach (9.3.1).

whyNot.0: The approach describes the procedure; specific risks are still recorded in the risk register.
whyNot.2: Projects tailor the approach to their context, which includes adopting the business's existing standards.
whyNot.3: The board approves the approach in DP, but that does not explain why using council standards is right.

reteach.title: Planning a family barbecue
reteach.question: Rain might spoil a barbecue. Which choices are avoid, reduce, transfer, accept and contingent plan, and who decides how much risk is acceptable?

blocks.body: Holding it indoors avoids the rain risk entirely. Putting up a gazebo reduces the impact if it rains. Paying a caterer who refunds you if it is rained off transfers the cost. Doing nothing and watching the forecast is accept. Booking the village hall as a fallback, used if it rains, is a contingent plan. Grandma, who is paying, decides how much risk the family will take: that is the appetite. The organizer then works within limits set from it.

blocks.text: The response must suit the appetite. If Grandma says 'no risk of a washout at all', simply watching the forecast is not good enough.

explain.body: A good risk is described as cause, event and effect, so others can understand and assess it. A vague label is not enough.

test.q: Calderbrook's Permits Online project is in discovery and alpha. Project manager Hannah Okoro has entered a risk in the register that reads simply: 'IT health check.' What should she do to improve the entry?
options: Describe its cause, event and effect
Move it into the risk management approach
Give it a response before assessing it
Raise it as an issue for the board
test.why: Identification includes describing each risk as cause, event and effect so it can be understood and assessed (9.3.1).

whyNot.1: The approach holds the procedure, not individual risks.
whyNot.2: Responses are planned after the risk is assessed, not before.
whyNot.3: Nothing has happened yet, so it is not an issue; it needs a clear risk description.

explain.body: Avoid removes the cause, so the threat can no longer happen. Reduce takes action now to lower probability or impact, leaving a residual risk.

test.q: Tarnside College's project faces the threat that construction traffic could strike students on the pedestrian route. The board approves redesigning site access so that all site traffic uses a separate rear gate and never crosses the pedestrian route. Which response is this, and why?
options: Reduce, because the probability falls
Accept, because the risk is still watched
Avoid, because the cause is removed
Transfer, because the contractor is liable
test.why: Avoid makes the situation certain by removing the risk; with no crossing, the cause of the threat is gone (table 9.1).

whyNot.0: Reduce leaves a residual risk; here the crossing that causes the threat is removed altogether.
whyNot.1: Accept means no action now, but a definite redesign has been made.
whyNot.3: Transfer moves financial impact to a third party; here the threat itself is removed.

explain.body: Proximity bias: near-term risks seem more important than later ones. Optimism bias: assuming success. Groupthink: harmony over dissent. Loss aversion: fearing a loss more than valuing a gain.

test.q: At a Wenmoor Community Health board review, members spend most of the meeting on the threat that an old fax machine fails next week. A much larger threat, that Moorside GP practices refuse to use the new route in six months' time, is not discussed. Which decision bias is most evident?
options: Groupthink
Proximity
Loss aversion
Optimism bias
test.why: Proximity bias is treating near-term situations as riskier and more important than later ones (9.2.4).

whyNot.0: Groupthink is putting harmony before dissent; nothing suggests members are suppressing doubts.
whyNot.2: Loss aversion is weighting losses over gains, which is not what is described.
whyNot.3: Optimism bias is assuming success; the board is focusing on the wrong timescale.

explain.body: The business states its appetite, often in words such as 'low' or 'moderate'. The project board turns that into measurable risk tolerances for its stages.

test.q: Carrowford City Council's risk policy sets a low appetite for public safety risk. The half marathon project is about to enter its build-up stage. Who should turn this into a measurable risk tolerance for that stage?
options: The corporate risk manager
The cabinet member for leisure
The project manager
The project board
test.why: Risk tolerance is set by the project board based on the business's risk appetite, and stage tolerances are the board's to set (9.2.1, 11.2.1).

whyNot.0: The corporate risk manager supports the council's policy but does not set the project's stage tolerances.
whyNot.1: The cabinet member champions the event; stage tolerances are set by the project board.
whyNot.2: The project manager works within stage tolerances and sets work package tolerances.
